items.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I talked to Jay Jay Johnson. He felt just like that. He could play everything. He says, “I’m still learning.”

ctx.x: Olympia Theatre. Boy, you must have been there. We went into the Olympia Theatre with Art Blakey and Kenny Clarke. It was fantastic. These two drummers. Oooooo boy. I’m telling you. You live for things like that. Both of these guys. You want to stop playing and just listen to them. It was great. Kenny Clarke. As I told you yesterday, he recorded with Miles on Prestige. Jay Jay Johnson, [Thelonious] Monk, and a few other people – Lucky Thompson. He played an eight-bar intro on Blue ’n Boogie. When drummers ask me,…

items.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: It was Kenny Dorham, J. J. Johnson, Wynton Kelly, and Paul Chambers. He was the drummer. ... that was the only time we actually played together.

ctx.x: . . . We wrote the drum stuff out, and he played it. Max was a good drummer. He was a nice friend. I never really played with him. I only did that recording. He did it with me. I forgot the name of it now, but it was for Riverside. It was Kenny Dorham, J. J. Johnson, Wynton Kelly, and Paul Chambers. He was the drummer. He had to go by the name of Spider Maxwell, because – but that was the only time we actually played together. When

I played with him, then I got the sense of what he was doing, because I was leaning on that while I was playing. He was an excellent drummer. He did things that you didn’t always expect to hear. So his mind was always in tune with the future, I say. He had one foot in the present and one foot in the future, and he had many ways of expressing himself: the double quartet; what was that? the Boom? . . .

items.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewer mentions Benny Golson as part of a group influenced by the interviewee's sessions, but the interviewee does not mention Golson directly or describe a personal interaction.

ctx.x: It was just a brilliant situation that I have never forgotten.

Let me follow through on that with Jimmy Heath. There are two sessions that you did, actually three. First of all, I’m sure you are already aware that what you did with the three horns on these two sessions set the tone for Gigi Gryce, Benny Golson, Quincy [Jones], and all of them. The album I’m talking about [is] the one where you used Jimmy Heath, where you do C.T.A. and Dear Old Stockholm. [Miles Davis, vol. 1. Blue Note BLP 1501]
